Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\rho_*>0$, $c_*>0$, and let $z_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ and $v_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be smooth periodic data on the normalized torus $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$. Use normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, coefficients $\widehat f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and componentwise norms $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat f(k)|^2$. To define the tangent system, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be any $C^2$ function with $P^{\prime}(\rho_*)=c_*^2$ (for example, $P(\rho)=c_*^2\rho$). The base nonlinear equations are $\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and $u_t+u\cdot\nabla u+\rho^{-1}\nabla P(\rho)=0$, for smooth positive scalar $\rho$ and vector $u$ on spacetime. The equilibrium is $(\rho,u)=(\rho_*,0)$. By its tangent system we mean that the derivative at $\epsilon=0$ of each equation residual evaluated at $(\rho,u)=(\rho_*+\epsilon z,\epsilon v)$ vanishes; the perturbation fields are arbitrary smooth maps, and $\epsilon$ is restricted near zero on each compact time interval so that density stays positive. The resulting constant-coefficient tangent system
$$z_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v=0,\qquad v_t+(c_*^2/\rho_*)\nabla z=0,\qquad (z,v)|_{t=0}=(z_0,v_0)$$
has a unique real $C^\infty$ solution $(z,v)$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d$. For every integer $m\ge0$, the weighted energy $\|v(t)\|_{H^m}^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)\|z(t)\|_{H^m}^2$ is constant for all $t\in\mathbb R$. This is the exact linear tangent model; it does not assert equality with a finite-amplitude nonlinear fluid evolution.

proof_steps.text: The mass residual at $(\rho_*+\epsilon z,\epsilon v)$ is $\epsilon(z_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v)+\epsilon^2\operatorname{div}(zv)$. The velocity residual is $\epsilon v_t+\epsilon^2v\cdot\nabla v+\epsilon[P^{\prime}(\rho_*+\epsilon z)/(\rho_*+\epsilon z)]\nabla z$. Differentiating at zero gives exactly the two displayed linear equations because $P^{\prime}(\rho_*)=c_*^2$. Thus the tangent interpretation follows from the defined residual derivative, without assuming that perturbations solve the nonlinear system for nonzero $\epsilon$. [given, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: The mass residual at $(\rho_*+\epsilon z,\epsilon v)$ is $\epsilon(z_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v)+\epsilon^2\operatorname{div}(zv)$. The velocity residual is $\epsilon v_t+\epsilon^2v\cdot\nabla v+\epsilon[P^{\prime}(\rho_*+\epsilon z)/(\rho_*+\epsilon z)]\nabla z$. Differentiating at zero gives exactly the two displayed linear equations because $P^{\prime}(\rho_*)=c_*^2$. Thus the tangent interpretation follows from the defined residual derivative, without assuming that perturbations solve the nonlinear system for nonzero $\epsilon$.

proof_steps.text: Write Fourier coefficients with kernel $e^{-ik\cdot x}$. For each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, the PDE is the finite-dimensional ODE $\dot{\widehat z}=-i\rho_* k\cdot\widehat v$, $\dot{\widehat v}=-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\widehat z$. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. At $k=0$ both coefficients are constant. [given, F1, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: Write Fourier coefficients with kernel $e^{-ik\cdot x}$. For each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, the PDE is the finite-dimensional ODE $\dot{\widehat z}=-i\rho_* k\cdot\widehat v$, $\dot{\widehat v}=-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\widehat z$. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. At $k=0$ both coefficients are constant.

proof_steps.text: Differentiation of these formulas recovers both mode equations and their initial coefficients. For each $k$, differentiating $E_k=|\widehat v|^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)|\widehat z|^2$ gives zero: the two cross terms are $-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)[(k\widehat z)\cdot\overline{\widehat v}+(k\cdot\widehat v)\overline{\widehat z}]$, whose bracket is real, so its real part vanishes. Thus $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ for every mode. The mode formulas also preserve conjugate symmetry because their coefficients at $-k$ are conjugates of those at $k$. [step 1.2, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: Differentiation of these formulas recovers both mode equations and their initial coefficients. For each $k$, differentiating $E_k=|\widehat v|^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)|\widehat z|^2$ gives zero: the two cross terms are $-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)[(k\widehat z)\cdot\overline{\widehat v}+(k\cdot\widehat v)\overline{\widehat z}]$, whose bracket is real, so its real part vanishes. Thus $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ for every mode. The mode formulas also preserve conjugate symmetry because their coefficients at $-k$ are conjugates of those at $k$.

proof_steps.text: Multiplying $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ by $(1+|k|^2)^m$ and summing over $k$ proves the stated conserved weighted energy by Parseval [F2]. Since the initial data are smooth, these sums are finite for every integer $m$; therefore the coefficient families remain in every $H^m$, uniformly for all time. [step 2.1, F1, F2]
proof_steps.claim: Multiplying $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ by $(1+|k|^2)^m$ and summing over $k$ proves the stated conserved weighted energy by Parseval [F2]. Since the initial data are smooth, these sums are finite for every integer $m$; therefore the coefficient families remain in every $H^m$, uniformly for all time.

proof_steps.text: Fourier synthesis [F2], under the stated Countable Choice assumption [A1], now defines real fields $z(t),v(t)$. The uniform $H^m$ bounds and embeddings [F3] imply convergence of the Fourier series with every spatial derivative, locally uniformly in time. The mode equations pass through these convergent series and give the PDE. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$. Thus all mixed derivatives are continuous, so $q\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d)$. [step 3.1, F2, F3, A1]
proof_steps.claim: Fourier synthesis [F2], under the stated Countable Choice assumption [A1], now defines real fields $z(t),v(t)$. The uniform $H^m$ bounds and embeddings [F3] imply convergence of the Fourier series with every spatial derivative, locally uniformly in time. The mode equations pass through these convergent series and give the PDE. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$. Thus all mixed derivatives are continuous, so $q\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d)$.

proof_steps.text: For any two smooth solutions with the same data, each Fourier-mode difference solves the same linear ODE with zero initial value. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional linear ODE gives zero difference at each $k$, and Fourier synthesis then gives equality of the fields. Together with the energy conservation and smooth synthesis above, this proves the global existence, conservation, and uniqueness assertions. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2] ∎
proof_steps.claim: For any two smooth solutions with the same data, each Fourier-mode difference solves the same linear ODE with zero initial value. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional linear ODE gives zero difference at each $k$, and Fourier synthesis then gives equality of the fields. Together with the energy conservation and smooth synthesis above, this proves the global existence, conservation, and uniqueness assertions.

proof_steps.text:
For each scalar component $f$ of the smooth initial data and every integer $N\ge0$, periodic integration by parts gives $(1+|k|^2)^N\widehat f(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^Nf}(k)$, where $\Delta=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2$; opposite periodic-face terms cancel. Since $(1-\Delta)^Nf$ is continuous on the compact torus, its $L^1$ norm $C_{f,N}$ is finite, and $|\widehat f(k)|\le C_{f,N}(1+|k|^2)^{-N}$.
For any integer $m\ge0$, choose $N$ with $4N-2m>d$. The shell $j\le|k|<j+1$ contains at most $C_d(j+1)^{d-1}$ lattice points, by placing disjoint unit cubes at its lattice points inside a shell of fixed enlarged width, so $\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{m-2N}<\infty$ by comparison with $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{d-1+2m-4N}$. Thus every initial component belongs to every $H^m$ under [F1].
Multiplying the mode identity $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ from step 2.1 by $(1+|k|^2)^m$ and summing these nonnegative finite-energy series proves, by [F2], the stated conserved weighted energy. In particular both coefficient families remain in every $H^m$, uniformly for all real time. [given, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

proof_steps.text: Fourier synthesis [F2], under the stated Countable Choice assumption [A1], now defines real fields $z(t),v(t)$. The uniform $H^m$ bounds and embeddings [F3] imply convergence of the Fourier series with every spatial derivative, locally uniformly in time. The mode equations pass through these convergent series and give the PDE. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$. Thus all mixed derivatives are continuous, so $q\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d)$. [step 3.1, F2, F3, A1]

proof_steps.text: For any two smooth solutions with the same data, each Fourier-mode difference solves the same linear ODE with zero initial value. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional linear ODE gives zero difference at each $k$, and Fourier synthesis then gives equality of the fields. Together with the energy conservation and smooth synthesis above, this proves the global existence, conservation, and uniqueness assertions. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2] ∎

public_sections.Statement: Let $d\ge1$ and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. Write $D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $D_0(\Omega)=\{h\in D(\Omega):\int_\Omega h=0\}$. For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

proof_steps.text: For each interval, choose an affine copy of the bump in [A1]. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. Its integral is finite and positive, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$. [given, A1, A2, algebra]

Its integral is finite and positive, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$.

proof_steps.text:
For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Then $\int H=0$ by [A2]. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define
$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$
Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other components are compactly supported by induction. [given, A1, A2, step 1.1, induction]

proof_steps.text: If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of $\theta_i$; for the first component also include the interval hull of these supports. The recursive formulas then place every output component inside the fixed compact product $K'=\prod_iJ_i$. Every output derivative is a finite sum of fixed-bump derivatives times finite-coordinate integrals of derivatives of $h$ or its marginals. Such integrals have sup norm at most the interval length times the integrand sup norm, and differentiation in other coordinates commutes with integration. Induction therefore bounds each output seminorm by a constant times finitely many input seminorms. This proves fixed-support continuity. [given, A1, A2, step 2.1, induction] ∎

proof_steps.text:
For the given rectangle, fix once for all inputs and support sets an affine copy of the bump in
[A1] on each side interval. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of
rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than
every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. By [F1] its continuous compact-interval integral exists; positivity makes it nonzero, so
normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. The primitive
difference quotient differs from $h(x)$ by at most $\sup\{|h(s)-h(x)|:s\text{ lies between }x\text{
and }x+\delta\}$, which tends to zero by continuity. Its derivative is therefore $h$, and it
vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its
support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the
zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$. [given, A1, F1, F4, algebra]

proof_steps.text:
Here and below the coordinate integrals of smooth compactly supported functions may be computed
on the closed coordinate intervals after extension by zero. This extension is smooth on a
neighborhood of the closed box: compact support leaves a neighborhood of every boundary face where
the function is zero. By [F1] the function and every coordinate section are Riemann integrable;
[F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box
integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal
to $\int_\Omega h$. [given, F1, F2]
proof_steps.claim:
Here and below the coordinate integrals of smooth compactly supported functions may be computed
on the closed coordinate intervals after extension by zero. This extension is smooth on a
neighborhood of the closed box: compact support leaves a neighborhood of every boundary face where
the function is zero. By [F1] the function and every coordinate section are Riemann integrable;
[F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box
integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal

proof_steps.text:
To differentiate a marginal, fix all other coordinates and restrict the differentiated
coordinate to a compact interval inside its open side interval. The integrand and each parameter
derivative are continuous on the resulting compact two-variable rectangle, so repeated [F3] gives
$$\partial_{x'}^\beta H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}\partial_{x'}^\beta h(s,x')\,ds,\qquad \sup|\partial^\beta H|\le (b_1-a_1)\sup|\partial_{x'}^\beta h|.$$
The inequality follows from [F4] with the second integrand zero. Continuity of these derivatives
jointly in the remaining parameters follows from the same bound applied to their differences and
uniform continuity of the integrand derivative on each compact box. [given, F3, F4]

The inequality follows from [F4] with the second integrand zero. Continuity of these derivatives

proof_steps.text:
The same reasoning differentiates an integral with upper endpoint $x_1$ in its other parameters.
For its $x_1$ derivative, the difference quotient of $\int_{a_1}^{x_1}f(s,x')\,ds$ differs from
$f(x_1,x')$ by at most $\sup_{s\text{ between }x_1\text{ and }x_1+\delta}|f(s,x')-f(x_1,x')|$, which
tends to zero by continuity; higher endpoint derivatives then follow by ordinary differentiation.
This proves the finite-integral identities used in the recursion. [given, F3, F4, step 1.3]

For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. By step 1.2, $\int
H=\int h=0$, and steps 1.3–2.1 show that $H$ and the displayed primitives are smooth. Assuming the

If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly
contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the
support of the already fixed bump $\theta_i$. Their product is a common compact output-support set
$K'=\prod_iJ_i$: before the first-coordinate support the primitive is zero, and after it the

proof_steps.text:
Write $p_m(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup|\partial^\alpha f|$, taking the maximum also over
components for vector fields, and put $\ell_1=b_1-a_1$. Step 1.3 gives $p_m(H)\le\ell_1p_m(h)$. For
the first component in step 3.1, a derivative with no $x_1$ differentiation is an integral of
$\partial_{x'}^\beta h-\theta_1\partial_{x'}^\beta H$ and is bounded by
$\ell_1(1+\ell_1\|\theta_1\|_\infty)p_m(h)$. If the derivative differentiates $x_1$ at least once,
the endpoint identity in step 2.1 gives a derivative of $h$ minus a fixed derivative of $\theta_1$
times a derivative of $H$, again bounded by a constant times $p_m(h)$. For each remaining component
$\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')$, the product derivative is bounded by a fixed bump-derivative
constant times $p_m(R'H)\le C'_m p_m(H)$ by induction. The dimension-one bounds in step 1.1 start
this induction. Thus
$$p_m(Rh)\le C_m p_m(h)\qquad(m\ge0),$$
where $C_m$ depends only on the fixed rectangle, bumps, dimension and $m$, not on $h$. These are all
fixed-support seminorm estimates, proving the full stated continuity. Every displayed construction
is linear in $h$, and the bumps were fixed once independently of $h$ and $K$, so the same map $R$
serves all compact input supports. [given, A1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1,
induction] ∎

public_sections.Definition: Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. If $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

proof_steps.text: Under $x=2\pi y$, normalized measure on $\mathbb T^d$ pushes forward to $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$ on $Q_d$, while $e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$ becomes $e^{ik\cdot x}$. Thus Fourier coefficients and the componentwise $L^2$ inner product are unchanged by this rescaling. [given, F2, F3, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: Under $x=2\pi y$, normalized measure on $\mathbb T^d$ pushes forward to $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$ on $Q_d$, while $e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$ becomes $e^{ik\cdot x}$. Thus Fourier coefficients and the componentwise $L^2$ inner product are unchanged by this rescaling.

proof_steps.text: Apply [F4] to each of the $N$ components after this rescaling. The coefficient map identifies scalar $L^2(Q_d)$ isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$; summing the component identities gives the vector-valued coefficient isometry. The Countable Choice hypothesis is exactly [F1]. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1]
proof_steps.claim: Apply [F4] to each of the $N$ components after this rescaling. The coefficient map identifies scalar $L^2(Q_d)$ isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$; summing the component identities gives the vector-valued coefficient isometry. The Countable Choice hypothesis is exactly [F1].

proof_steps.text: Since $w_k^{2s}>0$, symmetric truncations to $|k|_\infty\le M$ converge in the weighted $\ell^2$ norm by convergence of the defining nonnegative series. The conjugate-symmetry condition is preserved by these cutoffs, so the completion is exactly the real weighted coefficient subspace. For $s\ge0$, $w_k^{2s}\ge1$, hence the coefficient sequence is in $\ell^2$ and [F4] gives its unique $L^2$ representative. For $s<0$ the construction gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim. [given, F4, step 2.1] ∎

For $s<0$ the construction gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim.

Since $w_k^{2s}>0$, symmetric truncations to $|k|_\infty\le M$ converge in the weighted $\ell^2$ norm by convergence of the defining nonnegative series. The conjugate-symmetry condition is preserved by these cutoffs, so the completion is exactly the real weighted coefficient subspace. For $s\ge0$, $w_k^{2s}\ge1$, hence the coefficient sequence is in $\ell^2$ and [F4] gives its unique initially complex $L^2$ class. For each component $f$ of this class, complex conjugation preserves $L^2$ and the normalized coefficient convention gives
$$\widehat{\overline f}(k)=\overline{\widehat f(-k)}=\overline{a_{-k}}=a_k=\widehat f(k),$$
where $a_k$ is its coefficient coordinate. Uniqueness of Fourier synthesis in [F4] therefore gives $f=\overline f$ almost everywhere, so $\operatorname{Re}f$ is a real representative with the same coefficients. Applying this to the finitely many components gives a real $\mathbb R^N$-valued representative, unique up to equality almost everywhere by the coefficient isometry in step 2.1. For $s<0$ the construction gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim. [given, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

public_sections.Definition:
Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

public_sections.Statement:
Use Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval of absolute time in seconds and $E$ is an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space measured in metres. A Newtonian Cartesian inertial chart consists of this absolute-time coordinate and an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$. Write $I_3$ for the $3\times3$ identity matrix and set $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Inertial-chart changes have the form $t'=t+t_0$, $x'=Qx+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is constant. A frame in this statement means such an adapted chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Fix one such chart and a nonempty open spatial coordinate region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. All derivatives below are Cartesian derivatives in this fixed chart; the positive coordinate rescaling defined below is not a change of observer.

For a scalar field $f$, $\nabla_x f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$.

For a vector field $u=(u_i)$, define $D_xu,D:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\operatorname{div}_xu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $\Delta_xu,D_tu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ by $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\operatorname{div}_xu=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $(\Delta_xu)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u$. The fields $D$ and $\operatorname{div}_xu$ have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Fix constants $\rho_0>0$, $\mu>0$, $U>0$, $L>0$, and $c>0$, and define $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, $\operatorname{Re}=UL/\nu$, and $\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$. In SI units, $[u]=[U]=[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[x]=[L]=\mathrm m$, $[\rho]=[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=[P(\rho)]=[p_{\mathrm{ref}}]=[\sigma]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\Theta]=[X]=[\operatorname{Re}]=[\operatorname{Ma}]=1$; thus the two ratios are dimensionless.

Define the dimensionless coordinates and their domains by
$$\Theta=\frac{Ut}{L},\qquad X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad I^*=\left\{\frac{Ut}{L}:t\in I\right\},\qquad \Omega^*=\left\{\frac{x}{L}:x\in\Omega\right\}.$$
The map $\Phi:I\times\Omega\to I^*\times\Omega^*$, $\Phi(t,x)=(Ut/L,x/L)$, is bijective with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)=(L\Theta/U,LX)$. The corresponding $X$-derivatives are defined by the same component formulas.

In the first, force-free branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time partial derivatives and continuous first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let the pressure field $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Let the density field $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ be the constant $\rho_0$. Assume $\operatorname{div}_xu=0$ and the selected incompressible Newtonian equations
$$\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}_x\sigma,\qquad (\operatorname{div}_x\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij},$$
where $\sigma:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is stress, $p$ is the constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure, and the tension-positive stress convention identifies $\sigma n$ as traction on an outward unit normal $n$. Define $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{1}{U}u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr),\qquad p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{p\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},$$
for a constant reference pressure $p_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb R$. The scaled fields are dimensionless, $[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*]=1$, and have respectively the same stated velocity and spatial-pressure regularity. Equivalently, $u(t,x)=Uu^*(\Theta,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)$. The governing equations become exactly
$$\partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{inc}}^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

public_sections.Postulate:
Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an orientation-preserving affine isometry $X:M\to\mathbb R^3$ paired with that time coordinate. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s=\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho}$. Thus $\gamma$ is dimensionless, sound speed has units of metres per second, and pressure has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. The corresponding numerical state is $U(t,x):=(\rho(t,x),m(t,x),E(t,x))\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\gamma>1$, set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\},\qquad p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right).$$
Since $\rho(t,x)>0$ and $e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)>0$, $U(t,x)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. For this state, $E-m^2/(2\rho)=\rho e_{\mathrm{int}}$ and $p(U(t,x))=p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)$, so the numerical and thermodynamic pressure maps agree. With $u=m/\rho$, its one-dimensional Euler flux and isentropic sound speed are
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$
The components of $F$ are mass flux in kilograms per square metre second, momentum flux in pascals, and energy flux in watts per square metre. The speed $c$ is in metres per second.

Adopt the inviscid one-dimensional branch with zero body acceleration, zero specific heat supply, zero conductive heat flux, and isotropic three-dimensional Cauchy stress $\sigma=-p_{\mathrm{th}}I_3$ in the tension-positive convention in which traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; here $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Its restriction to the selected axis is the scalar normal stress $\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}:=\sigma_{11}=-p_{\mathrm{th}}$ in pascals, so the one-dimensional momentum flux is $\rho u^2-\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}=\rho u^2+p_{\mathrm{th}}$. In the following weak identities, write $p:=p_{\mathrm{th}}$. Assume the locally integrable conservative variables, fluxes, entropy density, and entropy flux satisfy the identities in the distributional sense. Let $\rho_0,m_0,E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ be the initial mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, momentum density in kilograms per square metre second, total energy density in joules per cubic metre, and entropy density in joules per cubic metre kelvin, respectively. Require all displayed densities, fluxes, and products to be locally integrable up to $t=0$: their absolute values have finite integrals on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using the fields for $t>0$. This requirement assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Test functions $\phi,\psi,\eta,\zeta\in C^1(\Omega\times[0,T_f))$ are compactly supported in space-time and vanish near $T_f$; $\zeta$ is nonnegative, and tests may be nonzero at $t=0$. Then adopt
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\,\partial_x\phi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho u\,\partial_t\psi+(\rho u^2+p)\partial_x\psi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\psi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(E\,\partial_t\eta+u(E+p)\partial_x\eta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
and
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+\rho u s\,\partial_x\zeta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$
The last inequality is a separately adopted physical entropy inequality. It is not deduced from the conservative equations or from smooth-flow identities. This postulate specifies a physical model and its idealized local-equilibrium closure; it does not assert existence or uniqueness of a weak solution, prove that actual matter obeys the model, or identify a computed state with an experimental observation.

public_sections.Definition:
Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. A measurable function on an open Euclidean set $D$ is locally integrable if its norm has finite Lebesgue integral on every compact subset of $D$. For a space-time field on $\Omega\times[0,T)$ this condition is imposed on compact subsets in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields are identified when they agree almost everywhere. Let $U: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$, $F: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^{m\times3}$, and $S: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$ be such fields, and let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally integrable. For each row $a$, define $(\operatorname{div}_x F)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$ in the distributional sense, and define $F:\nabla_x\phi=\sum_{a=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^3F_{aj}\partial_{x_j}\phi_a$. The equation $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ with distributional initial datum $U_0$ means that for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T);\mathbb R^m)$, continuously differentiable up to $t=0$ and supported away from $\partial\Omega$ and $t=T$,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\phi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$

No boundary condition on $\partial\Omega$ is encoded because the test fields are supported away from it. This initial identity specifies the initial datum distributionally; it does not assert $U(\cdot,t)\to U_0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ or any other stronger trace topology. Such a trace must be assumed or proved separately. The fields are abstract mathematical variables; no physical unit system or balance postulate is imposed.

For locally integrable scalar fields $H,R,H_0$ and a locally integrable flux $Q: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^3$, the inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_x Q\ge R$ with initial datum $H_0$ means that for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T))$ with the same support convention,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+Q\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega H_0(x)\psi(x,0)\,dx\le0.$$

Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L_n,\lambda_n)$, where $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\mathcal L_E:=\{E\cap B:B\in\mathcal L_n\}$ and the measure $\lambda_E(A):=\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\lambda_E$-null set. Nonnegative integrals are suprema of nonnegative simple minorants; signed real integrals are the difference of the positive- and negative-part integrals when those parts are finite. Finite-dimensional integrals are taken componentwise.

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $D:=\Omega\times[0,T)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ in spatial-first coordinates $(x,t)$. Both $D$ and $\Omega$ are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. Spatial integrals use $\lambda_\Omega$ from $\lambda_3$, and space-time integrals use $\lambda_D$ from $\lambda_4$. For a finite coordinate array $v$, set $\|v\|_1:=\sum_i|v_i|$, summing all entries for a matrix. A measurable field $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is locally integrable when $\int_K\|f\|_1\,d\lambda_E<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq E$. For $E=D$ the compact sets are taken in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields on $D$ are identified up to $\lambda_D$-almost-everywhere equality, and initial fields on $\Omega$ up to $\lambda_\Omega$-almost-everywhere equality. The slice $\Omega\times\{0\}$ is contained in a Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb R^4$; values of a space-time representative on that slice do not determine the separately prescribed initial field.

In the displayed weak identities, $\int_0^T\int_\Omega f\,dx\,dt$ denotes the joint integral of the zero extension of $f$ from $D$ with respect to $\lambda_4$. For each test, its compact support bounds the test and its first derivatives, so every component of the tested products is measurable and is bounded in absolute value by a fixed multiple of the norm of a locally integrable field on that compact set. Thus all tested products and their finite sums have finite signed integrals. Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ is the completed product of $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_1$; completed-product Fubini therefore also gives the displayed iterated notation, with section integrals taken for almost every time and set to zero on a measurable exceptional null set. No integrability of every individual time slice is required. The integral is unchanged by the stated almost-everywhere identifications. The same conventions apply to the scalar inequality and to the initial integrals on $\Omega$.

Let $U: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$, $F: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^{m\times3}$, and $S: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$ be such fields, and let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally integrable. For each row $a$, define $(\operatorname{div}_x F)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$ in the distributional sense, and define $F:\nabla_x\phi=\sum_{a=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^3F_{aj}\partial_{x_j}\phi_a$. The equation $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ with distributional initial datum $U_0$ means that for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T);\mathbb R^m)$, continuously differentiable up to $t=0$ and supported away from $\partial\Omega$ and $t=T$,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\phi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$

No boundary condition on $\partial\Omega$ is encoded because the test fields are supported away from it. This initial identity specifies the initial datum distributionally; it does not assert $U(\cdot,t)\to U_0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ or any other stronger trace topology. Such a trace must be assumed or proved separately. The fields are abstract mathematical variables; no physical unit system or balance postulate is imposed.

For locally integrable scalar fields $H,R:D\to\mathbb R$ and $H_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a locally integrable flux $Q: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^3$, the inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_x Q\ge R$ with initial datum $H_0$ means that for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T))$ with the same support convention,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+Q\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega H_0(x)\psi(x,0)\,dx\le0.$$

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Let $J\subset(0,T)$ and $D\subset\mathbb R^2$ be open, and let $h\in C^1(J\times D)$ have graph $\Gamma=\{(t,x',x_3):(t,x')\in J\times D,\ x_3=h(t,x')\}$ contained in an open patch $\mathcal O\subset (J\times D\times\mathbb R)\cap((0,T)\times\Omega)$. Here $x=(x',x_3)$ and all space-time points in this lemma use time-first coordinates $(t,x)$; the coordinate permutation $(t,x)\mapsto(x,t)$ identifies these fields and tests with the spatial-first domains in the conservative weak-form definition. The minus and plus sides are $\mathcal O^-=\mathcal O\cap\{x_3<h(t,x')\}$ and $\mathcal O^+=\mathcal O\cap\{x_3>h(t,x')\}$. Let $U^\pm,S^\pm$ be $\mathbb R^m$-valued and $F^\pm$ be $\mathbb R^{m\times3}$-valued fields that are $C^1$ on their respective sides and admit $C^1$ one-sided extensions to every relatively compact part of $\Gamma$. For a matrix flux $F$, $F_j\in\mathbb R^m$ denotes its $j$th spatial column and $(\operatorname{div}_xF)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$. For any one-sided trace $G$, write $[G]=G^+-G^-$. Put $\lambda=\sqrt{1+|\nabla_{x'}h|^2}$, and define the unit normal from minus to plus and its signed normal speed by
$$n=\frac{(-\nabla_{x'}h,1)}{\lambda},\qquad V_n=\frac{\partial_t h}{\lambda}.$$
Interpret $U,F,S$ as the ordinary locally integrable piecewise functions defined by their side values and traces; no singular measure supported on $\Gamma$ is added to $S$. The interior weak identity for $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ is the test identity of the conservative weak-form definition for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$. It holds if and only if $\partial_tU^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xF^\pm=S^\pm$ on both sides and
$$[F]n-V_n[U]=0$$
on $\Gamma$. The initial-data term in the weak initial form is independent; this interior jump condition neither asserts nor requires a strong trace at $t=0$.

For scalar fields $H^\pm,R^\pm$ and vector fluxes $G^\pm$ with the same piecewise $C^1$ regularity, the interior weak inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_xG\ge R$ means
$$\int_{\mathcal O}\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+G\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\le0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\mathcal O)$. It holds if and only if $\partial_tH^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xG^\pm\ge R^\pm$ on both sides and
$$[G]\cdot n-V_n[H]\ge0$$
on $\Gamma$. These are local equivalences for prescribed piecewise-smooth fields, not existence or uniqueness theorems for nonlinear systems. The fields are abstract mathematical variables with no assigned physical units or constitutive model.

public_sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice: every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Let $J\subset(0,T)$ and $D\subset\mathbb R^2$ be open, and let $h\in C^1(J\times D)$ have graph $\Gamma=\{(t,x',x_3):(t,x')\in J\times D,\ x_3=h(t,x')\}$ contained in an open patch $\mathcal O\subset (J\times D\times\mathbb R)\cap((0,T)\times\Omega)$. Here $x=(x',x_3)$ and all space-time points in this lemma use time-first coordinates $(t,x)$; the coordinate permutation $(t,x)\mapsto(x,t)$ identifies these fields and tests with the spatial-first domains in the conservative weak-form definition. The minus and plus sides are $\mathcal O^-=\mathcal O\cap\{x_3<h(t,x')\}$ and $\mathcal O^+=\mathcal O\cap\{x_3>h(t,x')\}$. Let $U^\pm,S^\pm$ be $\mathbb R^m$-valued and $F^\pm$ be $\mathbb R^{m\times3}$-valued fields that are $C^1$ on their respective sides and admit $C^1$ one-sided extensions to every relatively compact part of $\Gamma$. For a matrix flux $F$, $F_j\in\mathbb R^m$ denotes its $j$th spatial column and $(\operatorname{div}_xF)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$. For any one-sided trace $G$, write $[G]=G^+-G^-$. Put $\lambda=\sqrt{1+|\nabla_{x'}h|^2}$, and define the unit normal from minus to plus and its signed normal speed by
$$n=\frac{(-\nabla_{x'}h,1)}{\lambda},\qquad V_n=\frac{\partial_t h}{\lambda}.$$
Interpret $U,F,S$ as the ordinary locally integrable piecewise functions defined by their side values and traces; no singular measure supported on $\Gamma$ is added to $S$. The interior weak identity for $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ is the test identity of the conservative weak-form definition for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$. It holds if and only if $\partial_tU^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xF^\pm=S^\pm$ on both sides and
$$[F]n-V_n[U]=0$$
on $\Gamma$. The initial-data term in the weak initial form is independent; this interior jump condition neither asserts nor requires a strong trace at $t=0$.

For scalar fields $H^\pm,R^\pm$ and vector fluxes $G^\pm$ with the same piecewise $C^1$ regularity, the interior weak inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_xG\ge R$ means
$$\int_{\mathcal O}\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+G\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt\le0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\mathcal O)$. It holds if and only if $\partial_tH^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xG^\pm\ge R^\pm$ on both sides and
$$[G]\cdot n-V_n[H]\ge0$$
on $\Gamma$. These are local equivalences for prescribed piecewise-smooth fields, not existence or uniqueness theorems for nonlinear systems. The fields are abstract mathematical variables with no assigned physical units or constitutive model.

proof_steps.text: By [A2] and [F2], $P$ and $P^{-1}$ preserve the Lebesgue sigma-algebra and measure. Pullback by $P$ bijects nonnegative simple minorants and preserves their level-set measures, so the nonnegative integral is preserved by its defining supremum; applying positive and negative parts gives the same conclusion for the integrable tested scalar products in [F1]. Thus the time-first coordinates and the spatial-first weak definition give the same test integrals. For a test $\phi$ supported in $\mathcal O$, apply the product rule to the space-time current $(U^\pm,F_1^\pm,F_2^\pm,F_3^\pm)$ separately on $\mathcal O^-$ and $\mathcal O^+$. Coordinatewise integration by parts in $t,x_1,x_2,x_3$ gives $\int_{\mathcal O}(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi)=-\int_{\mathcal O^-}W^-\cdot\phi-\int_{\mathcal O^+}W^+\cdot\phi-\int_{J\times D}K_{\rm graph}\cdot\phi(t,x',h(t,x'))\,dx'\,dt$, where $W^\pm=\partial_tU^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xF^\pm-S^\pm$ and $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]$. Compact support removes all outer-boundary terms; the remaining graph term is the difference of the two side conormal fluxes. [given, F1, F2, A1, A2, construct, algebra]

proof_steps.text: The unnormalised space-time conormal from minus to plus is $(-\partial_th,-\nabla_{x'}h,1)$. Its contraction with the jump current equals $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]=\lambda([F]\cdot n-V_n[U])$. Since $\lambda>0$, the graph coefficient vanishes exactly when $[F]\cdot n-V_n[U]=0$, and has the same sign as the scalar entropy jump coefficient. [given, algebra]

proof_steps.text: If the weak identity holds, choose tests supported wholly inside either side in step 1.1. Each continuous component of $W^\pm$ must vanish: a nonzero value would have a fixed strict sign on a small ball and contradict the identity for a nonnegative $C^1$ bump there. With these bulk terms zero, step 1.1 gives zero integral of $K_{\rm graph}$ against every trace of a test. Any compactly supported $C^1$ graph test $\zeta(t,x')$ extends to the patch as $\phi(t,x',x_3)=\zeta(t,x')\eta(x_3-h(t,x'))$, where $\eta$ is a $C^1$ cutoff with $\eta(0)=1$ and sufficiently small support. Such a uniform tube lies in $\mathcal O$ because the graph over $\operatorname{supp}\zeta$ is compact in this open patch. A nonzero component of continuous $K_{\rm graph}$ would have a fixed sign on a small graph patch and contradict the identity. Hence $W^\pm=0$ and $K_{\rm graph}=0$. Conversely, these equalities make the weak integral zero by step 1.1, and step 1.2 gives the stated jump condition. [step 1.1, step 1.2, given, F1, A1]

Conversely, these equalities make the weak integral zero by step 1.1, and step 1.2 gives the stated jump condition.

proof_steps.text: For the scalar inequality, step 1.1 gives the weak integral as the negative of the bulk integrals of $g^\pm=\partial_tH^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xG^\pm-R^\pm$ and the negative graph integral with coefficient $K_H=[G_3]-\partial_th[H]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[G_{1,2}]$. If both bulk residuals and $K_H$ are nonnegative, the weak integral is nonpositive for every nonnegative test. Conversely, a negative bulk residual at a point admits a nonnegative bump supported on that side and violates the weak inequality. If $K_H<0$ at a graph point, continuity gives a smaller graph patch where $K_H$ is bounded above by a negative constant. Choose a nonnegative test with fixed positive trace on that patch and support in a tube of width $\varepsilon$ about the graph. The negative interface contribution to the weak integral is positive and independent of $\varepsilon$, while the bounded bulk terms have magnitude $O(\varepsilon)$; for small enough $\varepsilon$ the weak integral is positive, a contradiction. Hence both the side inequalities and $K_H\ge0$ are necessary. Step 1.2 shows $K_H=\lambda([G]\cdot n-V_n[H])$, so the stated jump sign is equivalent. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, given, F1, A1] ∎

If both bulk residuals and $K_H$ are nonnegative, the weak integral is nonpositive for every nonnegative test. Conversely, a negative bulk residual at a point admits a nonnegative bump supported on that side and violates the weak inequality. If $K_H<0$ at a graph point, continuity gives a smaller graph patch where $K_H$ is bounded above by a negative constant. Choose a nonnegative test with fixed positive trace on that patch and support in a tube of width $\varepsilon$ about the graph. The negative interface contribution to the weak integral is positive and independent of $\varepsilon$, while the bounded bulk terms have magnitude $O(\varepsilon)$; for small enough $\varepsilon$ the weak integral is positive, a contradiction. Hence both the side inequalities and $K_H\ge0$ are necessary. Step 1.2 shows $K_H=\lambda([G]\cdot n-V_n[H])$, so the stated jump sign is equivalent.

public_sections.Example: At a fixed point, let $\rho\in[0,\infty)$ be mass density and let $u\in\mathbb R^3$ be velocity. In SI units, $\rho$ is measured in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and the momentum-density vector $M=\rho u$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. To use momentum density as a field in a conservative weak form, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and $T>0$, take measurable maps $\rho:\Omega\times[0,T)\to[0,\infty)$ and $u:\Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^3$, and require their product $U(x,t):=\rho(x,t)u(x,t)$ to be locally integrable, including near $t=0$. The vector $M$ above is a pointwise value of such a product, not itself a field. At $\rho=0$, distinct vectors $u_1\ne u_2$ both give $M=0$, so the momentum density does not determine velocity. At $\rho>0$, the relation has the unique inverse $u=M/\rho$. This is a pointwise algebraic example and makes no claim that any chosen fields solve a differential equation.

proof_steps.text: Choose $u_1=0$ and $u_2=e_1$, where $e_1=(1,0,0)$. They are distinct, but at $\rho=0$ their momentum densities satisfy $\rho u_1=0=\rho u_2$. Thus the map $u\mapsto\rho u$ is not injective when $\rho=0$. [given, F1, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: Choose $u_1=0$ and $u_2=e_1$, where $e_1=(1,0,0)$. They are distinct, but at $\rho=0$ their momentum densities satisfy $\rho u_1=0=\rho u_2$. Thus the map $u\mapsto\rho u$ is not injective when $\rho=0$.

proof_steps.text: If $\rho>0$ and $M=\rho u$, division by the positive scalar gives the unique recovery $u=M/\rho$. Hence the failure in step 1.1 is exactly the zero-density degeneracy, not a claim about positive density. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎
proof_steps.claim: If $\rho>0$ and $M=\rho u$, division by the positive scalar gives the unique recovery $u=M/\rho$. Hence the failure in step 1.1 is exactly the zero-density degeneracy, not a claim about positive density.

public_sections.Postulate:
Work in a classical Cartesian inertial frame with SI units on a fixed open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and time interval $(0,T_f)$, where $T_f>0$ is measured in seconds. Write $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for functions whose absolute value is integrable on every compact subset. Let all fields be measurable functions of $(t,x)$ on $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. Require $T>0$ almost everywhere wherever $q/T$ or $r/T$ is used. Let $\rho\ge0$ be mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $u$ velocity in metres per second, $\sigma$ Cauchy stress in pascals, $b$ body acceleration in metres per second squared, $e$ specific internal energy in joules per kilogram, $q$ outward-positive conductive heat flux in watts per square metre, $r$ specific heat supply in watts per kilogram, $T>0$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $s$ specific entropy in joules per kilogram kelvin. Set $E:=e+|u|^2/2$, use $t=\sigma n$ for traction and rowwise matrix divergence, and define the test-gradient by $(\nabla\psi)_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}\psi_i$ and the Frobenius product by $A:B:=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

A test function is a $C^1$ function on $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$, compactly supported in space-time and vanishing near $T_f$; it may be nonzero at $t=0$. Let scalar test functions be $\phi,\eta,\zeta$ and vector test function be $\psi$. Adopt as a separate weak-branch model assumption that the displayed conservative variables, fluxes and sources below belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and satisfy the following identities for every indicated test function. Initial conservative data $\rho_0,m_0,\mathcal E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ represent initial mass, momentum, total-energy and entropy densities; the initial terms specify distributional data and do not assert a strong trace.

Mass balance, for every scalar $\phi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\cdot\nabla\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Momentum balance, for every vector $\psi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma):\nabla\psi+\rho b\cdot\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\cdot\psi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Total-energy balance, for every scalar $\eta$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho E\,\partial_t\eta+(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)\cdot\nabla\eta+(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\eta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\mathcal E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Physical entropy inequality, for every nonnegative scalar $\zeta\ge0$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+(\rho s u+q/T)\cdot\nabla\zeta+(\rho r/T)\zeta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$

Every conservative density, product, flux and source displayed in these tests is required to be locally integrable up to $t=0$, including $\rho u\otimes u$, $\rho E u$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$, $q/T$ and $\rho r/T$: its absolute value has finite integral on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using its values for $t>0$. This condition assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Interior test functions impose no boundary condition; walls, thermal exchange, periodic identifications and stronger initial trace conditions are separate data. This weak mass/momentum/energy adoption and the physical entropy inequality are not inferred for arbitrary discontinuous or vacuum states from the smooth balance postulate. The source term and the sign of the entropy inequality use the outward-positive heat-flux convention above.

public_sections.Postulate:
Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open spatial region and $I=(0,T_f)$ a time interval in seconds, with $T_f>0$. Let $\Sigma$ be a $C^1$ moving interface in $\Omega\times I$ that locally is the graph $x_3=h(t,x_1,x_2)$ and separates minus and plus sides; here $C^1$ means that the graph function and its first coordinate partial derivatives are continuous. Let $n$ be the dimensionless Euclidean unit normal pointing from minus to plus, and let $V_n$ be the signed normal speed of $\Sigma$ in metres per second. For a field with one-sided traces, define $[g]:=g_+-g_-$. Let $\rho\ge0$ be mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $u$ velocity in metres per second, $\sigma$ Cauchy stress in pascals, $e$ specific internal energy in joules per kilogram, $q$ outward-positive heat flux in watts per square metre, $T>0$ absolute temperature in kelvins, $s$ specific entropy in joules per kilogram kelvin, $b$ body acceleration in metres per second squared, and $r$ specific heat supply in watts per kilogram. Set $E:=e+|u|^2/2$ in joules per kilogram. Assume these fields are $C^1$ on each side and, for every relatively compact interface patch, admit $C^1$ one-sided extensions to its closed sides; here $C^1$ means that the fields and all their first time and spatial coordinate partial derivatives are continuous on those extensions. In particular, the resulting one-sided traces are finite and continuous. Assume that all displayed products and sources are locally integrable. The sources are ordinary volume functions and have no measure concentrated on $\Sigma$. Use traction $t=\sigma n$, $(u\otimes u)_{ij}=u_i u_j$, and rowwise matrix divergence $(\operatorname{div}F)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}F_{ij}$.

On each side suppose the classical equations hold:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho s)+\operatorname{div}(\rho s u+q/T)\ge\rho r/T.$$

Adopt the separate weak mass, momentum and total-energy identities and physical entropy inequality. Their interior restrictions use compactly supported $C^1$ tests in $\Omega\times I$, away from $t=0$ and $t=T_f$. The full weak forms may also use tests nonzero at $t=0$ and include initial-data terms; those terms are separate data and are not determined by the interface jumps. The interior weak conservation equations across $\Sigma$ hold if and only if the side equations hold and

$$[\rho u]\cdot n=V_n[\rho],$$

$$[\rho u\otimes u-\sigma]n=V_n[\rho u],$$

$$[\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q]\cdot n=V_n[\rho E].$$

The interior weak physical entropy inequality holds across the interface if and only if it holds on both sides and

$$[\rho s u+q/T]\cdot n-V_n[\rho s]\ge0.$$

Equivalently, for any conservative density $U$ and flux $F$ above, the interface coefficient is $[F]\cdot n-V_n[U]$; it must vanish for conservation and be nonnegative for physical entropy. These conditions apply only to the specified piecewise $C^1$ fields and traces. They neither establish existence or uniqueness of a multidimensional shock solution nor extend smooth material equations through arbitrary nonsmooth fields.

public_sections.Statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. On the exterior domain $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ put $s=U\cdot x$ and define

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

This field is $C^2$ up to the spherical boundary from the exterior, $p$ is $C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u\to U$ uniformly in direction as $r\to\infty$. It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. For $n=x/a$ on $S_a=\{x:|x|=a\}$, put $D u=(\partial_j u_i)_{i,j}$ and form the stress $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(Du+(Du)^{\mathsf T})$. The formal resultant with this sphere orientation is

$$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Here the velocity is $C^2$ and pressure $C^1$ locally up to $S_a$, the displayed bounds hold uniformly in direction, and pressure is normalized by its limit $p_\infty$. The claim is for the Stokes equations only; it gives no finite-Reynolds-number error bound or exterior Navier–Stokes existence result. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_\infty$ in pascals, and the resultant in newtons.

proof_steps.text: For any radial scalar functions $A,B$, direct Cartesian differentiation with $\partial_i r=x_i/r$ and $\partial_i s=U_i$ gives $\operatorname{div}(AU+Bsx)=(s/r)(A'+r^2B'+4rB)$ and $\Delta(AU+Bsx)=(A''+2A'/r+2B)U+(B''+6B'/r)sx$. For the stated coefficients, $A'=3a/(4r^2)+3a^3/(4r^4)$, $A''=-3a/(2r^3)-3a^3/r^5$, $B'=9a/(4r^4)-15a^3/(4r^6)$, and $B''=-9a/r^5+45a^3/(2r^7)$. Substitution yields $A'+r^2B'+4rB=0$ and $\Delta u=-3aU/(2r^3)+9asx/(2r^5)$. Also $\nabla(s/r^3)=U/r^3-3sx/r^5$, so $\nabla p=\mu\Delta u$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

This field is $C^2$ up to the spherical boundary from the exterior, $p$ is $C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u\to U$ uniformly in direction as $r\to\infty$. It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. $$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Here the velocity is $C^2$ and pressure $C^1$ locally up to $S_a$, the displayed bounds hold uniformly in direction, and pressure is normalized by its limit $p_\infty$. The claim is for the Stokes equations only; it gives no finite-Reynolds-number error bound or exterior Navier–Stokes existence result.
